record.paper_title: Major open problems in chaos theory and nonlinear dynamics
record.context_brief: Coexistence in the paradox of plankton
record.original_question: Explain the paradox of plankton by constructing a mathematically and physically adequate model in which many species of phytoplankton can coexist while competing for only one or a few limiting nutrients in a turbulent fluid environment. The source frames the paradox as the tension between competitive exclusion, which suggests that only one or a few species should survive at equilibrium under a small number of limiting resources, and the observed coexistence of hundreds of plankton species. The open problem is to identify a dynamics, likely involving both ecological interactions and chaotic fluid transport, that accounts for this coexistence.

evidence.quote: Here we mention a few major open problems: 1. an effective description of chaos and turbulence, 2. rough dependence on initial data, 3. arrow of time, 4. the paradox of enrichment, 5. the paradox of pesticides, 6. the paradox of plankton.

According to the principle of competitive exclusion, the final equilibrium state should be taken over by one or a few species according to the limiting factors. On the other hand, in reality hundreds species of the plankton coexist. This paradoxical question was first raised by Hutchinson [7].
Since Hutchinson’s work, there have been many studies on the paradox [27]. The problem involves two branches of chaotic dynamics: fluids and ecology.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Resolve the paradox of the plankton by constructing a mathematically rigorous and physically realistic dynamical model that exhibits the following features:

(a) The model describes a population of N ≫ 1 phytoplankton species with densities u_i(x,t), i = 1,...,N, evolving in a bounded fluid domain Ω ⊂ R^d (d = 2 or 3) carrying an incompressible turbulent (or chaotic) velocity field v(x,t) with ∇·v = 0.

(b) The species compete for a small number k ≪ N of limiting nutrient resources c_j(x,t), j = 1,...,k, whose dynamics include diffusion, advection by v, consumption by the species, and an external supply.

(c) The coupled equations take the general advection–reaction–diffusion form
    ∂_t u_i + v·∇u_i = D_i Δu_i + u_i F_i(c_1,...,c_k) − m_i u_i,
    ∂_t c_j + v·∇c_j = D_j' Δc_j + S_j(x,t) − Σ_i α_{ij} u_i F_i(c_1,...,c_k),
with biologically meaningful growth functions F_i (e.g., Monod kinetics) and constants D_i, D_j', m_i, α_{ij} > 0.

(d) In the well-mixed (spatially homogeneous) limit, the model reduces to a competition system for which the classical competitive exclusion principle holds: at most k species persist at equilibrium.

(e) For the full spatially extended model with a generic chaotic/turbulent advection field v, prove that there exist parameter regimes in which a number of species ≫ k coexist for all time in the sense of persistence (e.g., liminf_{t→∞} ∫_Ω u_i dx > 0 for every i), and characterize the mechanism (e.g., chaotic mixing, filamental nonequilibrium structures, oscillatory or chaotic attractors) responsible for this coexistence.

The problem is to exhibit such a model, give a rigorous proof of long-term coexistence of arbitrarily many species under only k ≪ N limiting nutrients, and show that the explanation is both mathematically consistent and physically adequate for plankton communities in turbulent oceanic environments.
artifact.status_search_result: The paradox of the plankton remains an active and unresolved problem. Numerous partial mechanisms have been proposed since Hutchinson (1961), including chaotic competition dynamics (Huisman–Weissing), spatial heterogeneity, mesoscale turbulence, "kill-the-winner" viral dynamics, and stochastic effects. No single mathematically and physically complete model has been accepted as the definitive resolution, and ecologists continue to propose new solutions, indicating the problem is still open.

status_evidence.title: Paradox of the plankton - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Various competition and predation models suggest that even in homogeneous and constant environments plankton will never settle to equilibrium... interactions may give rise to oscillations and chaos.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed but no definitive resolution is universally accepted.

status_evidence.title: paradox of the 'paradox of the plankton'
status_evidence.snippet: Over the past five decades, ecologists have offered dozens of solutions to the paradox... ecologists continue to offer up novel solutions.
status_evidence.claim: The problem continues to attract new proposed solutions, indicating it is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Towards a resolution of 'the paradox of the plankton'
status_evidence.snippet: A brief overview of the proposed mechanisms.
status_evidence.claim: The literature is still focused on identifying mechanisms rather than presenting a settled resolution.
